Both connect Jesus' significance with Moses' law and the prophets. Luke has Jesus declare fulfillment and also names Psalms; Acts has Paul explain and persuade concerning Jesus from law and prophets. Psalms and the exact fulfillment declaration are not inserted into Acts.

Both describe the Lord opening an inner faculty to receive instruction. Jesus opens disciples' minds to Scripture; the Lord opens Lydia's heart to attend Paul's words. Recipients, mind/heart language and instruction settings remain distinct.
Both connect Christ's suffering or death and third-day rising with Scripture. Corinthians adds for our sins and burial; Luke introduces the statement with thus it is written.

Peter's Jerusalem proclamation of repentance and forgiveness in Jesus' name is a specific beginning corresponding to this commission. Acts also adds baptism and the Spirit's gift; one Jerusalem address is not treated as completing the mission to all nations.
Both appoint the followers as Jesus' witnesses. Acts adds Spirit-given power and the outward geography from Jerusalem; Luke refers to the preceding events and teaching as these things.

Both command remaining in Jerusalem for the Father's promise. Luke describes clothing with power from above; Acts explicitly identifies coming Spirit baptism. That explanation is compared without rewriting Luke's actual wording.

Both describe lifting hands over people and blessing them. Aaron's blessing follows specified offerings; Jesus' blessing accompanies His departure toward Bethany. The figures, rites and settings are not equated.

Both describe Jesus being lifted or carried up and departing from their sight. Luke places it during blessing; Acts adds the cloud and, in its wider context, forty days of appearances. No extra date is imposed on Luke's narration.

Both describe the followers returning to Jerusalem after Jesus' ascent. Luke adds worship and great joy; Acts names Olivet, an upper room and the praying company. The distinct location notices are not replaced with one another.

Both summaries describe continuing temple worship and praise of God. Acts adds shared meals, favor and the growing gathering after Pentecost; Luke concludes with temple blessing after the ascent. The summaries are not declared one dated occasion.

The second criminal's rebuke invoking fear of God and shared judgment was read. General fear-of-God teachings or the adjacent criminal's mockery do not independently reproduce this distinctive response.

The two travelers' conversation about the recent events was read. Mark's road appearance summary does not independently reproduce this conversation, and generic discussion while traveling adds no precise counterpart.
